item.title: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees On Cars
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from WGNA-FM: On November 23rd, New York State Governor Kathy Hochul announced Bill S.9348A/A.10411A. This bill aims to put money back in New Yorkers pockets by prohibiting any vehicle manufacturers, dealers, or third-party providers from charging consumers more money for locked services or subscription fees. This specifically targets newer vehicles that may lock pre-installed features (like heated seats or screen compatibility) behind a paywall or subscription service. This is becoming more and more of a problem as years go by, and consumers have been very vocal against the practice, but this is a tangible step that can be taken to end this practice before it gets too out of hand. [...] The bill will go into effect on February 27th, 2027. "No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car," said New York Attorney General Letitia James stated. "Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down."

item.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
item.description: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

item.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
item.description: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?

item.title: Google Is Finally Retiring the Nest App Early Next Year
item.description:
Google is shutting down its 15-year-old Nest app on January 25, 2027, requiring users to switch to Google Home to remotely control their smart home devices and receive notifications. "Then, on August 2, the company will retire Google Assistant on smart speakers and displays, with Gemini replacing the older tech for voice controls," reports Engadget. From the report: If you've yet to migrate your Nest devices to the Google Home app, the company says your existing settings and schedules will transfer over automatically. The only thing you need to manually move over are any custom clips you might have saved over the years. You can do this by visiting the Nest website before January 25 and clicking the "Download all" button. Google says it will automatically migrate Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to its newer Google Home Premium package. "You will receive an email closer to the date of transfer detailing your subscription information," the company adds. "The Nest app launched over 15 years ago, and home technology has changed a lot since then," Google says of the decision. "To give every Nest user Google's latest security protections and most advanced cyber defenses, plus new features from Gemini, we're bringing all Nest devices together in the Google Home app."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

It has to survive the long dry spells, and it has to make full use of the brief windows when water is plentiful. A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Volcani Institute shows that the prickly pear cactus has an unexpected way of doing both.

item.title: Trump Halts Army's Plans to Detonate Bomb-Making Chemicals In Iowa
item.description:
President Trump has ordered the military to halt plans to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. "Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January," reports Ars Technica. From the report: The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice's request to put a hold on the Army's permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
item.description:
President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report: [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. On Sunday night, Nvidia's board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang's reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks. In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang's biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump's key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues. On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia's action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company "made the correct and proper decision." The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Mr. Trump wrote.

item.title: YC Startup Working On 'Cost Per Kill' For Missiles
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he's not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator's fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. "I think missiles are the coolest thing," Dandzbergs tells WIRED. "A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up." In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about "attacking hard problems," breaking things down to "first principles," and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war -- a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. "He's a pretty exceptional person," says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. "I'm still somewhat in disbelief that we're talking about a 16-year-old." Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup's guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the "cost per kill." Dandzbergs hopes to demonstrate a prototype missile by December. Despite concerns about the ethical implications of autonomous weapons and his young age, he remains undeterred. "I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare," he says. "Please don't say I'm sacrificing my childhood," says Dandzbergs. "This is the childhood I dreamed of."

item.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
item.description:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports: A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network. Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road." Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."

item.title: Anthropic's Safety-Conscious Corporate Culture Still Envisions Superintelligent AI
item.description:
The Washington Post looks at Anthropic's "unique" corporate culture, where CEO Dario Amodei "leads his workforce through essays, long memos posted in Slack and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly known as 'Dario Vision Quests'... "The CEO's output has established a constellation of beliefs treated as obvious, urgent and righteous inside the company: AI that supersedes humans is inevitable, the United States must limit China's AI development, and Claude might be conscious." Inside this tight-knit culture, Anthropic staffers, who call themselves Ants, get to feel that they are working on the world's most urgent problems, with the smartest people, in a shared mission to safeguard humanity, according to interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with the company's ethos, including several current and former employees. At its core is a belief that Anthropic — and Amodei — know what's best for the world... "A pervasive thing at Anthropic is: We're going to put on our capes and we're going to be the responsible ones, and we're going to accrue great power, but ... because we're doing it responsibly, it's responsible to acquire more power," said a former employee who left the company this year and, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation from the company.... Its message to investors fit with a vision of the future that Amodei often sketches out for his staff, people familiar with the company said, in which AI companies have the power of nation-states. After nearly six years of telling his workers that powerful AI will force society's leaders to makep difficult decisions, Amodei is now one of the powers who must decide how to act, in a major test of the corporate culture he has created.... [Amodei] set out to create a more safety-conscious culture when he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six people from his inner circle, most of them from OpenAI. In an internal memo the following year, Amodei laid out the stakes. "The current trajectory of AI development makes me think that there's a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI will lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity," he wrote, referring to the concept of artificial general intelligence, previously unreported court records show. He added that truly capable AI "seems more powerful/dangerous than nuclear weapons." Amodei was careful about those he hired to work on that existential challenge. Recruits were screened with a "culture interview," even for back office and policy roles, according to former employees and an archived copy of the company's careers page... It's "a bit of an 'are you ready for the cult' interview," an Anthropic hiring manager texted the unsuccessful candidate, according to a screenshot reviewed by The Post... Before ringing in Anthropic's record initial public offering at Times Square in New York on Thursday, Amodei delivered a short speech with some of his greatest hits. "To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," Amodei said.

item.description:
Reuters reports: Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia's recent scandal, kept in contact with an official from China's top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday. Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the report said, citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters... Reuters points out that several U.S. officials "have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy..." "A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang for comment..." But the New York Times also reported U.S. intelligence agencies have gathered evidence "that Ms. Huang's business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency." American author/journalist Greg Palast has his own unconfirmed theory, speculating that maybe Alice Huang wasn't a romantic interest but the Nvidia CEO's "business conduit to the Chinese military industrial complex... arranging the secret handoff of roughly one in five Nvidia chips." Why did the two Huang's make the affair so obvious? If she's a spy, why flaunt it before TV cameras and paparazzi? Because Huang and Huang wanted you to know... If Jensen and this guy's wife are conspiring to move hot chips to China, they can't exactly talk about it over the phone or in emails. But the nonprofit GrapheneOS project has a new problem, reports the blog It's FOSS : GrapheneOS has accused Google of leaning on phone makers to keep away from the project. The claim came in a thread on X [Thursday], where the project says makers were questioned about working with it, then threatened over their Google app licensing.... The project says Google is working against GrapheneOS itself and expects it to go further. It sees Pixel bootloaders being locked down eventually and Play Integrity, an API it calls illegal, being pushed harder. And if that were to happen, Android forks would struggle to survive under that. GrapheneOS believes some of Google's conduct breaks US criminal law and that antitrust violations can put individuals in prison. It wants to talk to the [U.S.] Department of Justice and says earlier cases against Google left its most serious violations largely untouched. Supporters are being asked for introductions to prosecutors and regulators, with assurances that the project has the necessary resources to carry on no matter what happens. item.description:
"A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks," reports The Hill, "amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure." The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.'s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with "hundreds if not thousands" of attacks per day, according to reporting from the Financial Times. The port's chief executive, Kent Britton, told the outlet that attacks surged from "known bad actor" countries and organizations that are searching for high-profile targets. ["Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure," the Financial Times reports.] The attacks against Corpus Christi's port went after its computer systems by attempting to find weaknesses. Attackers also sent phishing messages, posing as senior executives, to trick staff into allowing them access, per the Financial Times... "They're poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities," Britton said. "With AI, it'll only get more complicated." He stated the port was seeking additional help from Washington but "if you're playing defence, you have to get it right every time ... if you're planning offence, you only have to get it right once." The Port of Los Angeles — the country's busiest port — similarly stated that in August it had stopped 120 million attempted attacks into its networks through network exploitation, credential harvesting and malware attacks, Bloomberg reported. Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, expressed that all potential attackers "have to do is to get it right one time" and that it was "front of mind every day." "The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months..." reports the Financial Times, "exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce." The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks... The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17% increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI... The agencies said the joint offshore security boardings on August 21 and 24 were to "ensure integrity of the vessel's operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised"... Ports are taking action to defend their waterways. The Port of Virginia, a major hub for consumer goods, agriculture and coal, said the threat of attacks is now "more acute because of the rise of AI". It is heavily investing in its cyber security team, with employees undergoing monthly training and drills with the US Coast Guard.... The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey is also investing heavily in cyber defence. A spokesperson said it has "multiple independent layers of protection" and "recovery plans with terminal operators and partners, so that critical operations can continue and cargo can keep moving". Other ports are reluctant to discuss the threat they face — and their defences. The Port of Oakland said it would not publicly discuss its "cyber security defences or protective measures", citing national security concerns. The article notes it's not just affecting U.S. ports. item.title: Have Investors Lost Their Faith in the AI Boom?
item.description:
"A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion," writes NPR, adding that "investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions." While the world embraced the AI boom ,"now many are having regrets," argues a Washington Post technology reporter: The AI boom's key ingredient has always been faith — that more money can be found to pay for it, that AI will keep rapidly improving, that the masses will come to love it, that business productivity and profits from AI are just around the corner. Faith is now in short supply... By mid-year, AI executives started to say that business customers were balking at the high prices charged by providers of cutting edge or "frontier" AI like Anthropic. Many businesses began to save money by hopscotching among a range of AI technologies, including low-priced options from Chinese companies... Investors began to rebel, too, against the trillions of dollars that AI companies are spending to construct data centers and provide them with computing equipment and electricity. Last month, Google's stock market value dropped by half a trillion dollars in a single day, when it seemed like even the rich technology leader would take longer than expected to see an AI financial payoff. Such stumbles by AI companies eroded faith in AI, said Howard Marks, an investor famous for predicting the dot-com bust. "It somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility," Marks told Bloomberg TV this month. Like many AI companies, Anthropic can't afford to cover its AI development costs. The company said it will keep coming back to investors for cash and needs a steady stream of customers to pay the $900 billion it owes in coming decades. Perhaps the biggest wild card for the AI boom is growing public resentment toward AI and data centers and widening fears of AI-enabled cyberattacks, human deaths and widespread job losses. In this month's midterm elections, Americans voted in a wave of elected officials who have been skeptical of the AI industry and construction of data centers. The results could slow the AI boom that's already hitting major bottlenecks, including difficulty lining up enough electricity to expand AI computer capacity... Diane Swonk, chief economist at the accounting firm KPMG, isn't surprised that the public is uneasy about AI. During the dot-com boom, she said that Americans' wages rose alongside corporate profits and U.S. inequality narrowed. By contrast the AI boom's economic and prosperity payoff has been uneven. "Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting," writes NPR, "just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000..."

item.title: Sellers are Closing Etsy Stores in Response to Its New AI Training Policy
item.description:
"I burned my Etsy shop to the ground this week," illustrator Aaron Millard posted on Instagram: 8 years, 11,200 sales, 3k+ reviews, hundreds in a customer base. Deleted. Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out (in Canada, anyways)... Etsy's new Terms of Use — going into effect December 15 — include this language in their section about "Your Content": You also recognize our legitimate interest in using it... This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy. "My work took years to learn and create," illustrator Millard wrote on Instagram. "I won't let it be stolen. It's not free fuel for an AI slop business model." Following Etsy's announcement "artists are shutting down their shops in droves," writes Cartoon Brew, "and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next." Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers. Etsy says it uses sellers' content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn't train models designed to copy artists' work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content... The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it's worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI. "In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update," writes PC Gamer, "saying it's not really like that at all... [T]hat 'we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity.'" "... we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools." As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data." That hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his update that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy users and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses... Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default — and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so users who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck. Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman said was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform.

item.title: The New 'Riemann Hypothesis' Proof Has Been Confirmed in Mathlib/Lean Communities
item.description:
"Experts say the claim checks out," reports the Guardian. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," reads Saturday's announcement on the Lean prover community blog: The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct... [Besides checking the code] The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean's official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean's logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit... We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof. "The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems," writes the Guardian, "even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems." "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Scientific American captured more mixed reactions Friday: As Massachusetts Institute of Technology mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "This is indeed an historic moment," Sutherland tells me today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean. "The world has changed.... I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration." Sutherland says that it's worth celebrating the human work behind the development of Lean and LLMs — and, for that matter, the millennia of mathematical achievements upon which today's advance rests. But processing the earthshaking reality of what has occurred "is going to take some time." "There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof," he says. "And I can't wait to dig into them. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think."

Microsoft did not reveal how many emails were affected or how many users received non-delivery reports. The final report also reveals that the outage disrupted several important email security capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Office. This means affected messages may not have been removed as quickly as usual. Microsoft also confirmed that users experienced problems opening URLs protected by Safe Links. Depending on their organization's security policies, some users may have encountered a "Skip verification" option when Safe Links attempted to check a URL... Microsoft also acknowledged that its first customer notification arrived approximately 20 minutes after the widespread impact began. It plans to improve automated outage notifications by the end of 2026 to improve communication. "Microsoft eventually restored the services about 12 hours later..."

item.title: Climate Change Talks Fall Apart In Final Hours Over Fossil Fuels
item.description:
NPR reports international climate talks "broke down in overtime hours, over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels." At Sunday's U.N. climate summit, "nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas." The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room... After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected — including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands. The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. item.title: Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions'
item.description:
"A handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets," warn two security developers at the Python Software Foundation. Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents? Yes, repeatedly... The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one... When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one. pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway... Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises. The issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets... Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell. Python's official security developer in residence Seth Larson joined PyPI safety/security engineer Mike Fiedler to remove these dangerous trigger, also applying the policies Python Software Foundation-stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, and pypi). "They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations. "On a GitHub Team or Enterprise plan, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it."

item.description:
Car-maker Aptera announced Thursday it "completed its first vehicle for sale to a customer, a milestone years in the making." Aptera's three-wheeled solar electric vehicle charges from solar panels integrated into its body, and it plugs in like any other electric vehicle. "This is the moment our team has worked toward for years," said Chris Anthony, Co-CEO of Aptera. "To Accelerator #1, and to every reservation holder and shareholder who believed in this vehicle: thank you. We're working to complete more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible..." "What excites me about Aptera is how innovation can redefine the way we use energy in everyday mobility," said Martin Hartono, CEO of GDP Venture [and the proud recipient of Aptera solar car #1]. "By combining solar technology, battery power and an ultra-efficient vehicle design, Aptera offers a compelling solution for people who want to minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances. As an early believer in Aptera, I am proud to be part of this milestone and to see this vision become a reality." "Excuse me while I go find a hat to eat," jokes the blog InsideEVs... Nothing against Aptera specifically, but when a company hangs around for 20 years, while exchanging ownership hands several times without actually producing anything for customers, I start to get skeptical. However, Aptera Motors just did what so many doubters thought it'd never do: It delivered a road-legal production vehicle to one of its first early investors... [Aptera] does offer a interesting concept for customers who don't have long commutes and leave their car parked outside for most of the day while they work. In addition to plugging in to recharge, doesn't it sound nice to recoup your morning commute mileage with the sun while you're in the office? Whether this three-wheeled rolling solar panel ends up being a hit or not, and whether Aptera can stick around long enough to become a successful automaker, will take much longer to learn. But actually delivering a production car is a good place to start. Seven weeks ago Aptera said its first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, reports Electrek, with customer deliveries in early 2027 "subject to financing."

item.description:
While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production." Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently... For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... [Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones. Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too. FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. item.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
item.description:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.) Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night." Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...." The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives. While some hope the AI-fueled attacks "will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention," according to the article, "many of those steeped in the ecosystem... have their doubts." "I'm a bit pessimistic," says Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. "I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it."

item.title: Earth has a New Moon
item.description:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

item.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED. "We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

item.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
item.description:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins. The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester. "We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

item.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
item.description:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years. 2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof Add a new headline to the list... 2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order. [...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...] The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone." "If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind. In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system. But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports: Just hours after AlpÃgeâ(TM)s claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. âoeIf any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this,â he wrote. âoeWe are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.â

item.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says. [...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027.

item.title: Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."
